07-Security/02-Kubernetes-Security-Primi:
### Introduction

Security in Kubernetes is layered. Everything starts at the API Server, because every action goes through it. This page maps the questions you must answer: who can access the cluster, and what can they do?

### Layers

```
 Client ─► [Authentication] ─► [Authorization] ─► [Admission] ─► API action
            who are you?        what may you do?    policy checks
```

### Hosts and components

- Secure the nodes: disable password SSH, use key-based login, disable root login.
- Keep the control plane reachable only by necessary networks.

### Authentication (who)

Mechanisms for the API Server:

- Static password / token files (basic, **not for production**, removed in modern versions).
- Client certificates (X509).
- External identity providers: LDAP, OIDC, Kerberos.
- Service accounts for machines.

### Authorization (what)

- **RBAC** (role based) - standard.
- **ABAC** (attribute based) - old, file-based.
- **Node authorizer** - for kubelets.
- **Webhook** - external service decides.
- `AlwaysAllow` / `AlwaysDeny` - testing.

### Other protections

| Area | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Communication | TLS between all components |
| Pod-to-Pod | NetworkPolicies (default: all allowed) |
| Workload | SecurityContext, Pod Security Standards |
| Images | Private registries, image pull secrets |
| Secrets | RBAC, encryption at rest |
| Admission | Admission controllers, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy |

### Key takeaways

- Authentication → authorization → admission, all at the API Server.
- Every lesson in this section implements one layer.
07-Security/03-Authentication:
### Introduction

Kubernetes has no user objects. Users are external identities, authenticated by credentials presented to the API Server. Service accounts are the only built-in "machine" identities.

### Types of accounts

| Type | Managed by | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| User | Outside Kubernetes (certs, tokens, OIDC) | Humans, admins |
| Service Account | Kubernetes objects | Pods / applications |

### Methods

#### Client certificates (most common for admins)

The user presents a certificate signed by the cluster CA. The CN becomes the username and O the group. This is how `kubeadm` creates `kubernetes-admin` (group `system:masters`).

#### Bearer tokens

- Service account tokens (JWT, mostly short-lived and projected).
- Static token file: `--token-auth-file`.
- Bootstrap tokens for `kubeadm join`.

#### Static password file (legacy)

```
password,user,uid,group
```

passed with `--basic-auth-file`. Removed from current Kubernetes; do not use.

#### External

OIDC (Google, Keycloak, Dex), webhook token authentication, authenticating proxy.

### Example: static token file (legacy / lab)

```
# /tmp/users/user-token-details.csv
token1,user1,u0001,group1
```

API Server option `--token-auth-file=/tmp/users/user-token-details.csv`, and if run as a Pod you must mount the file.

```bash
curl -v -k https://master:6443/api/v1/pods --header "Authorization: Bearer token1"
```

### Anonymous requests

`--anonymous-auth` allows unauthenticated requests (user `system:anonymous`). Authorization still applies; health endpoints use it.

### Checking who you are

```bash
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i create pods
kubectl config view
```

### Key takeaways

- Users aren't objects; credentials identify them.
- Certificates are the standard for humans; tokens for machines.
07-Security/04-TLS-Certificates:
### Introduction

An overview of why Kubernetes needs TLS certificates. Each component communicates over TLS, authenticated by certificates, both for encryption and for identity.

### Where certificates are used

```
 admin / kubectl ──► kube-apiserver ◄── scheduler, controller-manager
                         │ ▲                 (client certs)
                         ▼ │
                       etcd         kube-apiserver ──► kubelet
                                    kubelet ──► kube-apiserver
```

Servers have **server certificates**; clients have **client certificates**.

### Key takeaways

- Security of the cluster depends on the PKI.
- The next lessons explain TLS theory and then every certificate in a cluster.

### Certificate roles at a glance

| Who | Presents | Verified against |
|---|---|---|
| kube-apiserver (as server) | `apiserver.crt` | cluster CA |
| kubectl / admin | `admin` client cert | cluster CA |
| scheduler, controller manager, kube-proxy | client certs | cluster CA |
| kube-apiserver → etcd | `apiserver-etcd-client.crt` | etcd CA |
| kube-apiserver → kubelet | `apiserver-kubelet-client.crt` | cluster CA |
| kubelet (server) | kubelet serving cert | cluster CA |

### Why it breaks

Typical TLS failures in Kubernetes: expired cert, wrong CA, missing SAN (name or IP not listed), wrong file path in a manifest. The error text usually says `x509: certificate ...`.

```bash
kubeadm certs check-expiration
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates
```
07-Security/05-TLS-Basics:
### Introduction

TLS provides encryption in transit and authentication.

### Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption

| | Symmetric | Asymmetric |
|---|---|---|
| Keys | One shared key | Public + private key pair |
| Speed | Fast | Slow |
| Problem | Key distribution | Used to solve it |

A public key encrypts; only the matching private key decrypts. Public keys can be shared freely.

### The TLS handshake

```
 client                                   server
   │ ── hello ─────────────────────────►    │
   │ ◄── certificate (server public key) ── │
   │ verify cert is signed by trusted CA    │
   │ generate symmetric key, encrypt it     │
   │ ── with the server's public key ─────► │
   │      both now use the symmetric key    │
```

### Certificates and CAs

A **certificate** binds a public key to an identity (name), signed by a **Certificate Authority**. Browsers trust public CAs. Inside a cluster you run a **private CA**.

```
 file         role
 *.crt, *.pem public key / certificate
 *.key        private key
```

Generate a key and a signing request:

```bash
openssl genrsa -out my.key 2048
openssl req -new -key my.key -subj "/CN=my-server" -out my.csr
openssl x509 -req -in my.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -out my.crt -days 365
```

### Client certificates

Servers can also demand a client certificate (mutual TLS) to authenticate the client. Used heavily between Kubernetes components.

### PKI

Public Key Infrastructure: CAs, certificates, and the process of issuing and managing them.

### Key takeaways

- Asymmetric encryption exchanges a symmetric key.
- CA-signed certificates prove identity.
07-Security/06-TLS-in-Kubernetes:
### Introduction

A cluster has many certificates. Knowing which is which is key to troubleshooting.

### Certificate map

```
                 CA (ca.crt/ca.key)
        signs ───────┬──────────────────────┐
                     ▼                      ▼
 Server certificates              Client certificates
  apiserver.crt/key                admin.crt/key
  etcd server.crt/key              scheduler.crt/key
  kubelet server certs             controller-manager.crt/key
                                   kube-proxy.crt/key
                                   apiserver-etcd-client.crt/key
                                   apiserver-kubelet-client.crt/key
```

| Component | Role | Certificate |
|---|---|---|
| kube-apiserver | server | `apiserver.crt` |
| kube-apiserver | client of etcd | `apiserver-etcd-client.crt` |
| kube-apiserver | client of kubelets | `apiserver-kubelet-client.crt` |
| etcd | server | `etcd/server.crt` |
| etcd peers | server/client | `etcd/peer.crt` |
| kubelet | server | `kubelet.crt` |
| kubelet | client of API server | `kubelet-client-current.pem` |
| scheduler, controller manager, kube-proxy, admin | client | each own client cert |

### Multiple CAs

The cluster CA signs most; ETCD can use its own CA (`/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt`). The front proxy has another.

### Locations (kubeadm)

```
/etc/kubernetes/pki/
   ca.crt  ca.key
   apiserver.crt  apiserver.key
   apiserver-etcd-client.crt/key
   apiserver-kubelet-client.crt/key
   front-proxy-ca.crt ...
   sa.key  sa.pub                  # service account signing
   etcd/ca.crt  server.crt  peer.crt ...
/etc/kubernetes/*.conf              # kubeconfigs for admin, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet
/var/lib/kubelet/pki/               # kubelet certs
```

### Key takeaways

- Every component needs a cert; servers and clients.
- Know the files and where they live.
07-Security/07-TLS-in-Kubernetes-Certifi:
### Introduction

How to create certificates for a cluster yourself using OpenSSL (done automatically by kubeadm). Understand the pattern, because the CKA asks you to inspect and sometimes create them.

### 1. Create the CA

```bash
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 2048
openssl req -new -key ca.key -subj "/CN=KUBERNETES-CA" -out ca.csr
openssl x509 -req -in ca.csr -signkey ca.key -out ca.crt -days 3650
```

### 2. Client certificate (admin)

```bash
openssl genrsa -out admin.key 2048
openssl req -new -key admin.key -subj "/CN=kube-admin/O=system:masters" -out admin.csr
openssl x509 -req -in admin.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -out admin.crt
```

- `CN` is the user name.
- `O` is the group; `system:masters` gives full admin rights.

Other component names: `system:kube-scheduler`, `system:kube-controller-manager`, `system:kube-proxy`.

### 3. Using the certificate

```bash
curl https://kube-apiserver:6443/api/v1/pods --key admin.key --cert admin.crt --cacert ca.crt
```

or in a kubeconfig.

### 4. Server certificates

Need the right names. The API Server certificate must contain every name or IP clients use as **Subject Alternative Names**:

```
kubernetes, kubernetes.default, kubernetes.default.svc,
kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local, 10.96.0.1, <master IP>, <load balancer name/IP>
```

```ini
# openssl.cnf
[req]
req_extensions = v3_req
[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names
[alt_names]
DNS.1 = kubernetes
DNS.2 = kubernetes.default
IP.1 = 10.96.0.1
IP.2 = 192.168.5.10
```

```bash
openssl req -new -key apiserver.key -subj "/CN=kube-apiserver" -out apiserver.csr -config openssl.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in apiserver.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -out apiserver.crt -extensions v3_req -extfile openssl.cnf
```

### 5. Kubelet certificates

Server certs named after each node, and client certs with `CN=system:node:<nodename>` and `O=system:nodes`.

### Key takeaways

- CA first, then sign everything with it.
- CN = user, O = group, SANs for servers.
07-Security/08-View-Certificate-Details:
### Introduction

When something breaks, you inspect certificates to find wrong names, wrong CA, or expiry.

### Find which certificate a component uses

```bash
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep -E "crt|key|ca"
cat /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf
```

### Decode a certificate

```bash
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -text -noout
```

Items to check:

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| `Subject: CN=...` | Correct name |
| `X509v3 Subject Alternative Name` | All required names/IPs |
| `Validity: Not After` | Expiry |
| `Issuer` | Right CA |
| `Key Usage / Extended Key Usage` | Server vs client auth |

Quick expiry check:

```bash
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -enddate
kubeadm certs check-expiration
```

### Logs when certs are wrong

```bash
journalctl -u etcd.service -l                 # for services
kubectl logs etcd-master                      # for kubeadm
crictl ps -a ; crictl logs <id>               # when kubectl is down
```

### Typical failures

- API server can't talk to ETCD: wrong etcd cert path in its manifest.
- ETCD fails: wrong CA in `--trusted-ca-file`.
- Expired certs: all kubectl commands fail with "certificate has expired".

### Renewing

```bash
kubeadm certs renew all
kubeadm certs renew apiserver
```

then restart the control plane Pods (move manifests out and back, or restart kubelet).

### Key takeaways

- `openssl x509 -text -noout` and `kubeadm certs check-expiration` are the two tools.
07-Security/09-Certificate-Health-Check-:
### Introduction

A systematic way to audit certificates: list each certificate in a table and verify attributes. It's an organisation tool and helps in troubleshooting questions.

### Suggested table

| Component | Type | Cert path | CN | SAN | Org | Issuer | Expiry |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| kube-apiserver | server | /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt | kube-apiserver | kubernetes, kubernetes.default, svc, IPs | | kubernetes | |
| apiserver-etcd-client | client | .../apiserver-etcd-client.crt | kube-apiserver-etcd-client | | system:masters | etcd-ca | |
| apiserver-kubelet-client | client | .../apiserver-kubelet-client.crt | kube-apiserver-kubelet-client | | system:masters | kubernetes | |
| etcd server | server | .../etcd/server.crt | controlplane | localhost, IP | | etcd-ca | |
| scheduler | client | scheduler.conf | system:kube-scheduler | | | kubernetes | |

### How to fill it in

1. Find the path in the component's manifest.
2. `openssl x509 -in <path> -text -noout`.
3. Copy CN, SAN, Issuer, Not After.
4. Compare with what is expected.

### Key takeaways

- Auditing each certificate quickly shows mismatches (wrong CA, expired, missing SAN).
07-Security/10-Practice-Test-View-Certif:
### How to approach this lab

Questions ask for specific attributes of certificates, or why a component fails because of a bad certificate path.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane | grep -E "tls-cert|etcd-.*file|client-ca"
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -text -noout | grep -E "Subject:|Issuer|DNS|Not After"
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt -text -noout | grep -E "Subject:|Not After"
kubeadm certs check-expiration
```

### If the API Server is broken

```bash
crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver
crictl logs <id>
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep etcd
ls /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/
```

A wrong filename in the manifest (for example `etcd-ca.crt` instead of `ca.crt`) breaks the connection; fix it, wait for the Pod to be recreated.

### Tips

- CN, SAN and Issuer answer most questions.
- Fix manifests carefully; the kubelet restarts the Pod after saving.

### Worked example

Find the SANs of the API server certificate and its expiry:

```bash
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -text | grep -A1 "Alternative Name"
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -enddate
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt -noout -subject
```

If ETCD won't start: `grep -E "cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml`, then `ls /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd` and fix any name that doesn't exist (for example `server-certificate.crt`).

### Common mistakes

- Reading the wrong CA (ETCD has its own under `pki/etcd`).
- Not waiting for the kubelet to restart the static Pod after a manifest change.
07-Security/11-Certificate-API:
### Introduction

Instead of manually signing certificates with the CA key, Kubernetes has a **Certificates API** (CSR objects). Users submit a request, an admin approves it, and the controller manager signs it.

### Workflow for a new user

```
 user: key + csr ─► admin creates CertificateSigningRequest ─► approve ─► user gets certificate
```

1. User creates key and CSR:

```bash
openssl genrsa -out jane.key 2048
openssl req -new -key jane.key -subj "/CN=jane" -out jane.csr
```

2. Admin creates a CSR object (request is base64 of the file):

```bash
cat jane.csr | base64 -w 0
```

```yaml
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  name: jane
spec:
  request: <base64 here>
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client
  expirationSeconds: 86400
  usages:
  - client auth
```

3. Review and approve:

```bash
kubectl get csr
kubectl certificate approve jane
kubectl certificate deny jane
kubectl delete csr jane
```

4. Extract the certificate:

```bash
kubectl get csr jane -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > jane.crt
```

### Who does the signing

The **kube-controller-manager** (CSR-APPROVING and CSR-SIGNING controllers) uses the CA key and cert configured by:

```
--cluster-signing-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
--cluster-signing-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key
```

### After the certificate

Give the user permissions with RBAC and a kubeconfig entry:

```bash
kubectl config set-credentials jane --client-certificate=jane.crt --client-key=jane.key --embed-certs
kubectl create role ... ; kubectl create rolebinding ...
```

### Troubleshooting

- CSR stays `Pending`: not approved yet.
- Approved but no certificate: controller manager down or not configured with signing keys.
- `signerName` is required in v1.

### Key takeaways

- CSR object → approve → certificate is issued by the controller manager.
07-Security/12-Practice-Test-Certificate:
### How to approach this lab

Create a CSR for a user, approve it, and reject a suspicious one.

### Commands

```bash
cat akshay.csr | base64 -w 0
vi akshay-csr.yaml
kubectl apply -f akshay-csr.yaml
kubectl get csr
kubectl certificate approve akshay
kubectl get csr agent-smith -o yaml        # examine requested groups
kubectl certificate deny agent-smith
kubectl delete csr agent-smith
```

### Notes

- A CSR that requests `system:masters` is suspicious; deny it.
- `base64 -w 0` avoids line wraps in the YAML value.
- The CSR YAML needs `usages: ["client auth"]` and `signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client`.

### Worked example

```bash
cat akshay.csr | base64 -w 0
```

```yaml
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  name: akshay
spec:
  groups: [system:authenticated]
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client
  usages: [client auth]
  request: <paste base64>
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f akshay.yaml
kubectl get csr
kubectl certificate approve akshay
kubectl get csr agent-smith -o yaml | grep -A3 groups      # requests system:masters?
kubectl certificate deny agent-smith
```

### Common mistakes

- Line breaks inside the base64 string.
- Forgetting `signerName`.
07-Security/13-kubeconfig:
### Introduction

A kubeconfig file stores how to reach clusters and who you are, so you don't pass certificates on every command. Default location `$HOME/.kube/config`.

### Structure

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
current-context: dev-user@dev-cluster
clusters:
- name: dev-cluster
  cluster:
    server: https://dev:6443
    certificate-authority: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
    # or certificate-authority-data: <base64>
users:
- name: dev-user
  user:
    client-certificate: /path/dev.crt
    client-key: /path/dev.key
contexts:
- name: dev-user@dev-cluster
  context:
    cluster: dev-cluster
    user: dev-user
    namespace: dev
```

Three sections: **clusters** (where), **users** (who), **contexts** (cluster + user + namespace).

### Commands

```bash
kubectl config view
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config current-context
kubectl config use-context prod-user@production
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev
kubectl config set-cluster ...
kubectl config set-credentials ...
kubectl config set-context ...
kubectl config delete-context ...
```

### Using a different file

```bash
kubectl --kubeconfig=/root/my-kube-config get pods
export KUBECONFIG=/root/my-kube-config
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/other-config      # merged
KUBECONFIG=/root/my-kube-config kubectl config use-context research
```

To make a file the default, copy it to `~/.kube/config`.

### Certificates in a kubeconfig

Use paths (`certificate-authority`) or embed base64 (`certificate-authority-data`).

### Namespace in a context

A context can set a default namespace, which changes where `kubectl` commands apply.

### Troubleshooting

- "The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused": no kubeconfig found.
- Wrong server address or CA path: errors mention x509.
- Use `kubectl config view --minify` to see the active context only.

### CKA exam tips

- Many exam tasks begin with `kubectl config use-context <name>`; always run the command provided.

### Key takeaways

- Clusters + users + contexts; switch with `use-context`.
07-Security/14-Practice-Test-KubeConfig:
### How to approach this lab

Inspect the default kubeconfig, switch contexts, and repair a broken file.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl config view
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config use-context research --kubeconfig /root/my-kube-config
kubectl config current-context --kubeconfig /root/my-kube-config
export KUBECONFIG=/root/my-kube-config
vi /root/.kube/config          # fix path/typos
cp /root/my-kube-config /root/.kube/config
```

### Fixing a broken kubeconfig

Typical issue: the `certificate-authority` or client certificate path has a typo (`ca.crt` vs `ca.crt`), or wrong port. Compare to files in `/etc/kubernetes/pki/users/`.

### Notes

- Count entries: clusters, users, contexts via `kubectl config view`.
- `--kubeconfig` overrides the default location for that command.

### Worked example

```bash
kubectl config view --kubeconfig /root/my-kube-config
kubectl config get-contexts --kubeconfig /root/my-kube-config
kubectl config use-context research --kubeconfig /root/my-kube-config
kubectl config current-context --kubeconfig /root/my-kube-config
```

Make it the default:

```bash
cp /root/my-kube-config /root/.kube/config
```

Broken `kubectl get pods` ("unable to read certificate-authority ..."): compare the `certificate-authority:` path in `~/.kube/config` with `ls /etc/kubernetes/pki/` and fix the filename.

### Common mistakes

- Setting `KUBECONFIG` in one shell and testing in another.
- Using `use-context` without `--kubeconfig` when a non-default file is meant.
07-Security/15-API-Groups:
### Introduction

All Kubernetes capabilities are exposed through the REST API, organised into groups. Understanding groups is needed for RBAC rules (`apiGroups`).

### Two categories

| Category | Path | Resources |
|---|---|---|
| Core (legacy) | `/api/v1` | pods, namespaces, nodes, services, configmaps, secrets, PV, PVC, events |
| Named | `/apis/<group>/<version>` | apps, batch, networking.k8s.io, rbac.authorization.k8s.io, storage.k8s.io, certificates.k8s.io, policy, autoscaling |

```
/api/v1/pods
/apis/apps/v1/deployments
/apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/networkpolicies
/apis/certificates.k8s.io/v1/certificatesigningrequests
```

Within each group are **resources** and **verbs** (`list, get, create, delete, update, patch, watch`).

### Discovering

```bash
kubectl api-resources -o wide              # kind, group, namespaced, verbs
kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps
kubectl api-versions
curl http://localhost:8001/apis | grep name
kubectl proxy 8001 &
```

### Versions

`v1` (stable), `v1beta1` (beta, may change), `v1alpha1` (alpha, disabled by default). Preferred version is chosen by the API Server.

### Why it matters

An RBAC rule must name the right group:

```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]           # core group is the empty string
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get","list"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["create"]
```

### Key takeaways

- Core group is `""`; others have names; check with `kubectl api-resources`.
07-Security/16-Authorization:
### Introduction

Once authenticated, the API Server must decide whether the identity can perform an action. Authorization restricts users to the minimum permissions they need.

### Mechanisms

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| **Node** | Authorises kubelets (identities `system:node:<name>` in group `system:nodes`) to read what their Pods need |
| **ABAC** | Policy file of user/action pairs; must restart API Server to change; not recommended |
| **RBAC** | Roles bound to users/groups/service accounts; standard |
| **Webhook** | Ask an external service |
| AlwaysAllow / AlwaysDeny | Testing |

Set with:

```
--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC,Webhook
```

Modes are evaluated **in order**; the first that approves or denies decides. `Node` is checked first. If a mode says "no opinion", the next one is consulted. If none approve, the request is denied.

### Check the current mode

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane | grep authorization-mode
ps -aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep authorization
```

### Testing

```bash
kubectl auth can-i create deployments
kubectl auth can-i delete nodes
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as dev-user
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as dev-user --namespace test
kubectl auth can-i --list
```

### Key takeaways

- Node,RBAC is the kubeadm default.
- `kubectl auth can-i` verifies permissions.
07-Security/17-RBAC:
### Introduction

Role-Based Access Control grants permissions to roles, then binds roles to subjects (users, groups, service accounts).

```
 Subject ◄── RoleBinding ──► Role ──► rules (apiGroups, resources, verbs)
```

### Role (namespaced)

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: developer
  namespace: default
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["list","get","create","update","delete"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["create"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  resourceNames: ["web"]          # restrict to specific objects
  verbs: ["get","update"]
```

Imperative:

```bash
kubectl create role developer --verb=list,get,create --resource=pods -n default
kubectl create role dev --verb=get --resource=pods --resource-name=blue,orange
```

### RoleBinding

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: devuser-developer-binding
  namespace: default
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: dev-user
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: developer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

```bash
kubectl create rolebinding devuser-developer-binding --role=developer --user=dev-user
kubectl create rolebinding x --role=developer --group=devs
kubectl create rolebinding x --role=developer --serviceaccount=default:sa1
```

### Inspect

```bash
kubectl get roles
kubectl get rolebindings
kubectl describe role developer
kubectl describe rolebinding devuser-developer-binding
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as dev-user
```

### Key rules

- Roles and RoleBindings are **namespaced** and apply in their namespace only.
- Permissions are additive (no deny rules).
- `roleRef` is immutable after creation.
- A Pod can't get more rights than its service account.

### Troubleshooting

- "forbidden: User ... cannot list resource": missing role/binding, wrong namespace, wrong apiGroup, wrong verb.
- Mismatch between `kind: User` name and certificate CN.

### Key takeaways

- Role (what) + RoleBinding (who).
07-Security/18-Practice-Test-RBAC:
### How to approach this lab

Inspect existing RBAC, then grant or fix a user's permissions.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane | grep authorization
kubectl get roles
kubectl get rolebindings -A
kubectl describe role kube-proxy -n kube-system
kubectl describe rolebinding kube-proxy -n kube-system
kubectl get pods --as dev-user
kubectl create role developer --namespace=default --verb=list,create,delete --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding dev-user-binding --namespace=default --role=developer --user=dev-user
kubectl edit role developer -n blue        # add resources/apiGroups
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as dev-user -n blue
```

### Notes

- When a user can't create Deployments, add the `apps` group in a rule.
- `resourceNames` limits to named Pods.
- Always test with `--as`.

### Worked example

User `dev-user` must create, list and delete Pods in `default`, and manage Deployments:

```bash
kubectl create role developer --verb=create,list,delete --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding dev-user-binding --role=developer --user=dev-user
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as dev-user
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as dev-user       # no
kubectl edit role developer       # add apiGroups: ["apps"], resources: ["deployments"]
```

Inspect an existing grant:

```bash
kubectl describe rolebinding kube-proxy -n kube-system
kubectl describe role kube-proxy -n kube-system
```

### Common mistakes

- Role created in the wrong namespace.
- Missing `apps` group for Deployments.
- Using `--user=dev-user` on a role instead of a binding.
07-Security/19-Cluster-Roles:
### Introduction

Some resources are cluster-scoped (nodes, PVs, namespaces), and sometimes you want rights across all namespaces. For those use ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding.

### Namespaced vs cluster-scoped

```bash
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false
```

### ClusterRole

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-admin
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["nodes"]
  verbs: ["get","watch","list","create","delete"]
```

### ClusterRoleBinding

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: node-admin-binding
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: cluster-admin-user
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: node-admin
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

```bash
kubectl create clusterrole node-admin --verb=get,list,watch --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding node-admin-binding --clusterrole=node-admin --user=michelle
```

### Cluster role with a RoleBinding

A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole to grant its permissions **inside one namespace** (reuse of common roles).

### Built-in cluster roles

`cluster-admin`, `admin`, `edit`, `view`, plus system roles (`system:node`, `system:kube-scheduler`...).

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles | wc -l
kubectl describe clusterrole view
```

### Key takeaways

- ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding = cluster-wide access.
07-Security/20-Practice-Test-Cluster-Rol:
### How to approach this lab

Create a ClusterRole for nodes or storage and bind it to a user, then test.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles --no-headers | wc -l
kubectl get clusterrolebindings --no-headers | wc -l
kubectl describe clusterrolebinding cluster-admin
kubectl create clusterrole nodeadmin --verb=get,watch,list,create,delete --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding michelle-binding --clusterrole=nodeadmin --user=michelle
kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as michelle
kubectl create clusterrole storage-admin --resource=persistentvolumes,storageclasses --verb=get,watch,list,create,delete
kubectl create clusterrolebinding michelle-storage-admin --user=michelle --clusterrole=storage-admin
```

### Note

`storageclasses` live in the `storage.k8s.io` group; `kubectl create clusterrole` picks the group automatically from the resource name.

### Worked example

```bash
kubectl create clusterrole nodeadmin --verb=get,watch,list,create,delete --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding michelle-binding --clusterrole=nodeadmin --user=michelle
kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as michelle           # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as michelle          # no
```

Add storage rights later:

```bash
kubectl create clusterrole storage-admin --resource=persistentvolumes,storageclasses --verb=get,watch,list,create,delete
kubectl create clusterrolebinding michelle-storage-admin --user=michelle --clusterrole=storage-admin
```

### Common mistakes

- Using Role/RoleBinding for nodes or PVs (cluster scoped).
- Forgetting the binding after creating the role.
07-Security/21-Service-Account:
### Introduction

A service account (SA) is an identity for applications running in Pods, used to authenticate to the API Server.

### Basics

```bash
kubectl create serviceaccount dashboard-sa
kubectl get sa
kubectl describe sa dashboard-sa
```

Each namespace has a `default` SA that Pods use unless they specify another.

### Tokens

Modern clusters (v1.24+):

- Pods get a **projected, time-limited token** automatically mounted at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/` (token, ca.crt, namespace).
- No long-lived Secret is created automatically.
- Create a token on demand:

```bash
kubectl create token dashboard-sa
kubectl create token dashboard-sa --duration=1h
```

- Legacy long-lived token Secret (if needed):

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: sa-token
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/service-account.name: dashboard-sa
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
```

### Use in a Pod

```yaml
spec:
  serviceAccountName: dashboard-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false     # optional: don't mount a token
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
```

The SA of an existing Pod can't be changed; Deployments allow it by editing the template.

### Authorising a service account

```bash
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding sa-binding --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=default:dashboard-sa
```

Subject form: `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>`.

### Using the token from outside

```bash
TOKEN=$(kubectl create token dashboard-sa)
```

07-Security/23-Image-Security:
### Introduction

Images come from registries. Private registries need credentials, which a Pod provides through an image pull secret.

### Image names

```
nginx                          = docker.io/library/nginx:latest
myrepo/app:1.2                 = docker.io/myrepo/app:1.2
gcr.io/project/app:v3          = registry gcr.io
private-registry.io/apps/web   = private registry
```

Avoid `:latest`; pin tags or, better, digests (`image@sha256:...`).

### Using a private registry

1. Create a Docker registry secret:

```bash
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=private-registry.io \
  --docker-username=registry-user \
  --docker-password=registry-password \
  --docker-email=registry-user@org.com
```

2. Reference it in the Pod:

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: private-registry.io/apps/internal-app
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: regcred
```

The secret must be in the **same namespace** as the Pod.

### Pull policy

`imagePullPolicy`: `Always`, `IfNotPresent`, `Never`. Default: `Always` for `:latest` or no tag, `IfNotPresent` otherwise.

### Troubleshooting

```bash
kubectl describe pod x      # ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff: "pull access denied" or "not found"
kubectl get secret regcred -o yaml
```

Typical causes: typo in name/tag, missing secret, wrong namespace, expired credentials.

### Key takeaways

- docker-registry secret + `imagePullSecrets`.

07-Security/25-Security-Context:
### Introduction

A security context sets privilege and access control for a Pod or container: which user runs the process, Linux capabilities, filesystem restrictions.

### Pod level vs container level

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-pod
spec:
  securityContext:              # applies to all containers
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 3000
    fsGroup: 2000
  containers:
  - name: ubuntu
    image: ubuntu
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:            # overrides pod level for this container
      runAsUser: 1001
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        add: ["NET_ADMIN","SYS_TIME"]
        drop: ["ALL"]
```

**Capabilities** are only supported at the container level.

### Common fields

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `runAsUser`, `runAsGroup` | UID/GID of the process |
| `runAsNonRoot: true` | Refuse to start as root |
| `fsGroup` | Group owning mounted volumes |
| `privileged: true` | Nearly all host access (avoid) |
| `allowPrivilegeEscalation` | Block setuid gaining more privileges |
| `readOnlyRootFilesystem` | Immutable root filesystem |
| `capabilities` | Add/drop Linux capabilities |
| `seccompProfile`, `seLinuxOptions` | Kernel-level restrictions |

### Verify

```bash
kubectl exec web-pod -- whoami
kubectl exec web-pod -- id
kubectl exec web-pod -- ps aux
```

### Pod Security Standards

Namespace labels enforce `privileged`, `baseline`, or `restricted` profiles:

```bash
kubectl label ns dev pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
```

### Key takeaways

- Run as non-root, drop capabilities, read-only filesystem.

07-Security/27-Network-Policies:
### Introduction

By default every Pod can talk to every other Pod. A NetworkPolicy restricts traffic to and from selected Pods, like a firewall. It needs a CNI that enforces it (Calico, Cilium, Weave; Flannel does **not**).

### Traffic model

```
 Ingress: traffic INTO selected Pods
 Egress:  traffic OUT of selected Pods
```

Rules are **allow lists**. As soon as a Pod is selected by a policy for a direction, all traffic in that direction is denied except what is allowed.

### Example: only the API Pod may reach the DB on 3306

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-policy
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: db
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: api-pod
      namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: prod
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 192.168.5.10/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3306
```

### AND vs OR in `from`

```yaml
# OR: two list items
from:
- podSelector: {...}
- namespaceSelector: {...}

# AND: one item with both
from:
- podSelector: {...}
  namespaceSelector: {...}
```

This indentation detail is a frequent exam trap.

### Selectors available

- `podSelector` (Pods in the policy's namespace).
- `namespaceSelector` (all Pods in matching namespaces).
- `ipBlock` (CIDR, with `except`).

### Egress example

```yaml
policyTypes: [Egress]
egress:
- to:
  - ipBlock: {cidr: 192.168.5.10/32}
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
```

Remember to allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) if you restrict egress.

### Default policies

```yaml
# deny all ingress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
# allow all ingress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  ingress:
  - {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
```

### Commands

```bash
kubectl get netpol
kubectl describe netpol db-policy
kubectl get pods --show-labels
```

### Testing

```bash
kubectl exec -it web -- nc -zv db 3306
kubectl exec -it web -- curl -m 3 http://db:3306
```

### Troubleshooting

- Policy seems ignored: CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy.
- Everything blocked: you selected the Pod with `policyTypes` but no allow rule; add rules.
- Check labels on Pods and namespaces (namespace labels needed for `namespaceSelector`; `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` is automatic).

### CKA exam tips

- Practise writing these from the docs (search "NetworkPolicy").
- Remember AND/OR and DNS for egress.

### Key takeaways

- Selected Pods become default-deny for the listed directions; add allow rules.


```yaml
metadata:

spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      name: payroll
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
```

08-Storage/02-Introduction-to-Docker-Sto:
### Introduction

Before Kubernetes storage, understand how containers handle data. Containers are ephemeral; when they are removed their data goes with them unless it is stored outside.

### Two kinds of Docker storage

1. **Storage drivers / layered filesystem** - how image and container layers are stored.
2. **Volume drivers** - how persistent data is stored.

### Layered architecture

An image is a stack of read-only layers (one per Dockerfile instruction). A running container adds a thin writable layer on top.

```
 ┌───────────────────────┐
 │ container layer (R/W) │  deleted with the container
 ├───────────────────────┤
 │ image layer 4 (RO)    │
 │ image layer 3 (RO)    │
 │ image layer 2 (RO)    │
 │ image layer 1 (RO)    │
 └───────────────────────┘
```

Layers are cached and shared among images, which saves space and speeds builds.

**Copy-on-write**: modifying a file from an image layer copies it up into the writable layer first.

### Key takeaways

- Data in the writable layer is lost when the container is removed; use volumes.
08-Storage/03-Storage-in-Docker:
### Introduction

How Docker keeps data beyond the life of a container.

### Volumes and bind mounts

```bash
docker volume create data_volume           # /var/lib/docker/volumes/data_volume
docker run -v data_volume:/var/lib/mysql mysql      # volume mount
docker run -v /data/mysql:/var/lib/mysql mysql      # bind mount (host path)
docker run --mount type=bind,source=/data/mysql,target=/var/lib/mysql mysql
```

| Type | Location | Managed by |
|---|---|---|
| Volume mount | `/var/lib/docker/volumes/...` | Docker |
| Bind mount | Any host path | You |
| tmpfs | Memory | Host (non-persistent) |

If you use a volume name that doesn't exist, Docker creates it.

### Storage drivers

Docker chooses one based on the OS: `overlay2` (common), `aufs`, `zfs`, `btrfs`, `device mapper`. They implement the layered filesystem.

### Key takeaways

- Use volumes for persistence; drivers handle layers.
08-Storage/04-Volume-Driver-Plugins-in-D:
### Introduction

Volumes are handled by **volume driver plugins**. The default is `local`. Others can provide remote storage: Azure File Storage, GlusterFS, Portworx, NetApp, REX-Ray (AWS EBS, S3, Google Persistent Disk) and more.

```bash
docker run -it --name mysql --volume-driver rexray/ebs --mount src=ebs-vol,target=/var/lib/mysql mysql
```

This creates a volume on a cloud disk, persisting even if the host disappears.

### Key takeaways

- Plugins let containers use external storage backends.
- This is the precursor of the Kubernetes Container Storage Interface.

### Why this matters for Kubernetes

Docker's volume plugins hid storage details behind a driver. Kubernetes took the same idea further: instead of each runtime having plugins, the **CSI** standard lets any vendor ship a driver that works in any orchestrator. When you see `provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com` in a StorageClass, that's the descendant of a Docker volume driver.

```
Docker:       container ─► volume driver (rexray/ebs) ─► cloud disk
Kubernetes:   Pod ─► PVC ─► StorageClass ─► CSI driver ─► cloud disk
```
08-Storage/05-Container.Storage-Interfac:
### Introduction

Kubernetes originally had storage code built in for each backend. The **Container Storage Interface (CSI)** is a standard so any storage vendor can write a plugin without modifying Kubernetes.

### The three interfaces

| Interface | Standardises |
|---|---|
| CRI | Container runtimes (Docker, containerd, CRI-O) |
| CNI | Networking plugins |
| CSI | Storage plugins |

### What CSI defines

Remote procedure calls the orchestrator uses, such as `CreateVolume`, `DeleteVolume`, `ControllerPublishVolume`. The storage vendor implements them in a **CSI driver**, usually deployed as a controller Deployment plus a node DaemonSet.

```
 Kubernetes ──CSI RPC──► driver (Portworx, EBS, Ceph, NetApp...) ──► storage backend
```

### In practice

```bash
kubectl get csidrivers
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep csi
```

A StorageClass names the driver in `provisioner:`.

### Key takeaways

- CSI is the standard storage plugin API; it works with any container orchestrator.
08-Storage/06-Volumes:
### Introduction

A Pod's container filesystem is ephemeral. A **volume** attaches storage to a Pod that lives as long as the Pod (or longer, for external volumes) and is shared among its containers.

### Basic example

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo $(date) >> /opt/number.out; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /opt
      name: data-volume
  volumes:
  - name: data-volume
    hostPath:
      path: /data
      type: Directory
```

`volumes` defines the storage; `volumeMounts` places it in a container.

### Common volume types

| Type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `emptyDir` | Empty directory created when the Pod starts, deleted with the Pod; shared between containers; can be in memory (`medium: Memory`) |
| `hostPath` | Directory from the node's filesystem; data stays on that node; avoid on multi-node |
| `configMap`, `secret`, `downwardAPI`, `projected` | Inject configuration |
| `persistentVolumeClaim` | Use a PersistentVolume (next lessons) |
| `nfs`, `awsElasticBlockStore`, `csi`, ... | External storage |

### Why hostPath is limited

On a multi-node cluster, Pods may land on different nodes and see different data. Use real network or cloud storage via PVs.

### emptyDir sharing

```yaml
volumes:
- name: cache
  emptyDir: {}
```

Two containers in the Pod can mount it to exchange files.

### Key takeaways

- `volumes` + `volumeMounts`; volume types decide the backend.
08-Storage/07-Persistent-Volumes:
### Introduction

Defining storage in every Pod is not scalable. A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is a cluster-wide pool of storage created by an admin. Users claim from it using PVCs.

```
 Admin ─► PV (10Gi)       User ─► PVC (5Gi) ─► binds ─► Pod uses PVC
```

### PV definition

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-vol1
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: /tmp/data         # lab only
```

Production: replace `hostPath` with `nfs`, `csi`, cloud disk, etc.

### Access modes

| Mode | Short | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ReadWriteOnce | RWO | One node read/write |
| ReadOnlyMany | ROX | Many nodes read-only |
| ReadWriteMany | RWX | Many nodes read/write |
| ReadWriteOncePod | RWOP | One Pod only |

### Reclaim policy

What happens to the PV after its claim is deleted:

| Policy | Result |
|---|---|
| `Retain` (default for manual PVs) | PV stays, `Released`, data kept, needs manual cleanup |
| `Delete` | PV and backing storage are deleted (default for dynamic) |
| `Recycle` | Deprecated |

### Phases

`Available` → `Bound` → `Released` → (`Failed`).

```bash
kubectl get pv
kubectl describe pv pv-vol1
```

PVs are cluster-scoped (no namespace).

### Key takeaways

- PV = the storage resource; capacity, access mode, reclaim policy.
08-Storage/08-Persistent-Volume-Claims:
### Introduction

A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a user's request for storage. Kubernetes binds each PVC to a suitable PV.

### PVC

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: myclaim
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Mi
  storageClassName: manual
```

### Binding rules

The controller finds a PV where:

- `capacity` >= requested size
- access modes include the requested one
- `storageClassName` matches
- selectors/labels match if specified (`selector.matchLabels`)

Binding is **one to one**. A 1Gi PV bound by a 500Mi claim wastes the rest. If no PV matches, the PVC stays `Pending` (unless dynamic provisioning applies).

```bash
kubectl get pvc
kubectl get pv
kubectl describe pvc myclaim
```

### Deleting a PVC

Depends on the PV's reclaim policy (Retain/Delete). PVCs in use by a Pod are protected (`kubernetes.io/pvc-protection`) until the Pod is gone.

### Troubleshooting a Pending PVC

- Size too large for any PV.
- Access mode mismatch.
- `storageClassName` mismatch (even empty vs set).
- No PV available, and no default StorageClass.

### Key takeaways

- PVC requests, PV supplies; match on size, access mode, class.
08-Storage/09-Using-PVC-in-PODs:
### Introduction

Pods consume claims by referencing them in `volumes`.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: mypod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: "/var/www/html"
      name: mypd
  volumes:
  - name: mypd
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: myclaim
```

The same works for ReplicaSets and Deployments (in the Pod template). The PVC must be in the same namespace as the Pod.

### Check

```bash
kubectl get pod mypod
kubectl describe pod mypod       # Volumes section, events
kubectl exec mypod -- df -h /var/www/html
kubectl exec mypod -- sh -c 'echo hi > /var/www/html/x'
```

### Troubleshooting

- Pod `Pending`: unbound PVC or no schedulable node for the volume.
- `ContainerCreating`: mount failure; see events.
- Data gone: you used `emptyDir` or the PV was `Delete`/hostPath on another node.

### Key takeaways

- Pod → PVC → PV → storage.
08-Storage/10-Practice-Test-Persistent-V:
### How to approach this lab

Create a Pod with a hostPath volume, then a PV, a PVC, and use the claim.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl get pv,pvc
kubectl describe pvc claim-log-1
kubectl apply -f pv.yaml
kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml
kubectl get pvc          # STATUS Bound
kubectl delete pvc claim-log-1
kubectl get pv           # Released / Retain
```

### Notes

- A Pending PVC usually has a bigger request than the PV or a different access mode.
- Deleting a PVC used by a Pod: the PVC stays `Terminating` until the Pod is deleted.
- With `Retain`, the PV is `Released` and not reusable without cleanup.
- Remember `storageClassName` in both PV and PVC when set.

### Worked example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata: {name: pv-log}
spec:
  capacity: {storage: 100Mi}
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath: {path: /pv/log}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: claim-log-1}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources: {requests: {storage: 50Mi}}
```

The claim above stays `Pending`: the PV offers `ReadWriteMany` only. Change the claim to `ReadWriteMany` (PVCs can't be edited, so delete and recreate) and it binds.

```bash
kubectl get pv,pvc
kubectl delete pvc claim-log-1          # PV becomes Released (Retain)
```

### Common mistakes

- Different `storageClassName` on PV and PVC.
- Requesting more storage than the PV offers.
08-Storage/12-Storage-Class:
### Introduction

Manual PV creation does not scale. A **StorageClass (SC)** enables **dynamic provisioning**: when a PVC requests the class, the provisioner creates the storage and PV automatically.

```
 PVC (storageClassName: fast) ─► StorageClass fast ─► provisioner ─► disk + PV created ─► bound
```

### Definition

```yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: google-storage
provisioner: kubernetes.io/gce-pd
parameters:
  type: pd-ssd
  replication-type: none
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
```

### Fields

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `provisioner` | Driver that creates volumes (CSI driver name) |
| `parameters` | Provisioner-specific settings (type, IOPS) |
| `reclaimPolicy` | `Delete` (default) or `Retain` for created PVs |
| `volumeBindingMode` | `Immediate` or `WaitForFirstConsumer` (wait for a Pod to be scheduled) |
| `allowVolumeExpansion` | Allow resizing PVCs |

### PVC using the class

```yaml
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: google-storage
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Mi
```

### Default class

```bash
kubectl get sc                           # (default) marker
kubectl patch sc standard -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'
```

A PVC without `storageClassName` uses the default class; `storageClassName: ""` means no class (static binding only).

### Local storage

`provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner` plus `WaitForFirstConsumer` for local PVs, where you create PVs yourself.

### Key takeaways

- StorageClass = automatic PV creation with chosen parameters.
08-Storage/13-Practice-Test-Storage-Clas:
### How to approach this lab

Inspect classes and create a PVC and Pod that use a local StorageClass with delayed binding.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl get sc
kubectl describe sc local-storage
kubectl get pvc
kubectl describe pvc local-pvc          # Pending: waiting for first consumer
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml               # PVC binds once the Pod is scheduled
kubectl get pv
```

### Notes

- `WaitForFirstConsumer` keeps the PVC `Pending` until a Pod uses it; that is expected.
- `no-provisioner` means PVs are created by hand.
- Check the provisioner column and reclaim policy.

### Worked example

```yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: {name: delayed-volume-sc}
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
```

```bash
kubectl get pvc local-pvc          # Pending (waiting for first consumer) - normal
kubectl apply -f nginx-pod.yaml    # uses the PVC
kubectl get pvc,pv                 # Bound once the Pod is scheduled
```

### Common mistakes

- Treating a `WaitForFirstConsumer` Pending PVC as an error.
- Forgetting that `no-provisioner` needs a PV created by hand.
09-Networking/01-Networking-Introduction:
### Introduction

Kubernetes networking builds on ordinary Linux networking. This section first covers prerequisites (switching, routing, DNS, namespaces, Docker networking, CNI), then Kubernetes cluster networking, Pod networking, Services, DNS and Ingress.

### Roadmap

```
 prerequisites:  switching/routing ─ DNS ─ network namespaces ─ Docker networking ─ CNI
 cluster:        node ports, Pod network (CNI), Service network (kube-proxy)
 discovery:      CoreDNS
 exposure:       Services, Ingress
```

### Key takeaways

- If you know Linux networking basics, skip the prerequisites; otherwise they explain everything later.

### What you must be able to do by the end of this section

1. Explain how Pods get IP addresses and reach each other across nodes (CNI).
2. Explain what a ClusterIP is and how kube-proxy implements it.
3. Resolve Services by DNS and fix CoreDNS problems.
4. Expose applications with NodePort, Ingress or Gateway API.
5. Write NetworkPolicies (covered in Security).
6. Troubleshoot connectivity layer by layer.

### Connectivity debug ladder

```
 Pod → Pod IP        (CNI)
 Pod → Service IP    (kube-proxy, endpoints)
 Pod → Service name  (CoreDNS)
 outside → app       (NodePort / Ingress / Gateway)
```

Test from the bottom up and stop at the first layer that fails.
09-Networking/02-Pre-requisite-Switching:
### Introduction

How machines talk on a network.

### Switching

A **switch** connects hosts on one network (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24). Each host has an interface (`eth0`).

```bash
ip link                         # list interfaces
ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0
ip addr show
```

Hosts on the same network communicate through the switch without a router.

### Routing

A **router** connects different networks (192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24). It has an IP on each. Hosts need a route to tell them where to send traffic for other networks.

```bash
ip route                        # or route
ip route add 192.168.2.0/24 via 192.168.1.1
ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
```

### Gateway

The gateway is the router address a host uses to leave its network. The **default gateway** (`0.0.0.0/0`) handles anything with no specific route.

### Linux as a router

By default Linux does not forward packets between interfaces.

```bash
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward        # 0 = off
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
# permanent: /etc/sysctl.conf  net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
```

### Diagnostics

```bash
ping 192.168.2.5
traceroute 192.168.2.5
ip route get 192.168.2.5
```

### Key takeaways

- Switch = same network; router = between networks; route entries + gateways.
- IP forwarding must be enabled for a Linux router (and Kubernetes nodes need it).
09-Networking/03-Pre-requisite-DNS:
### Introduction

DNS maps names to IP addresses.

### Local name resolution

`/etc/hosts` maps names to IPs on a single machine:

```
192.168.1.11   db
```

For many hosts, use a DNS server. Point hosts at it in `/etc/resolv.conf`:

```
nameserver 192.168.1.100
search mycompany.com prod.mycompany.com
```

Order of lookup is in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` (`hosts: files dns`: files first, then DNS).

### Domain hierarchy

```
 root (.) ─► com ─► google ─► www
 www.google.com  = host www in domain google.com
```

`search` domains let you type `web` and resolve `web.mycompany.com`.

### Record types

| Type | Maps |
|---|---|
| A | name → IPv4 |
| AAAA | name → IPv6 |
| CNAME | name → another name (alias) |
| MX, TXT, SRV, PTR | mail, text, service location, reverse |

### Tools

```bash
ping web
nslookup www.google.com        # ignores /etc/hosts
dig www.google.com
host web
```

### Key takeaways

- Files, then DNS; `resolv.conf` sets the server and search domains.
09-Networking/04-Pre-requisite-CoreDNS:
### Introduction

CoreDNS is a flexible DNS server written in Go, and it's the default DNS in Kubernetes.

### Running it

```bash
wget https://github.com/coredns/coredns/releases/...
./coredns
```

It listens on port 53 and is configured with a **Corefile** made of plugins:

```
.:53 {
    errors
    health
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
        pods insecure
        fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
}
```

The `hosts` plugin can serve entries from a file, and `kubernetes` serves cluster records.

### Key takeaways

- CoreDNS = pluggable DNS configured by the Corefile.

### Worked example: a tiny local DNS server

```
# Corefile
. {
    hosts /tmp/hosts {
        fallthrough
    }
    forward . 8.8.8.8
    log
}
```

```
# /tmp/hosts
192.168.1.10   web.example.test
```

```bash
./coredns -conf Corefile
dig @127.0.0.1 web.example.test
```

Plugins run in the order defined by CoreDNS (not the file order), `fallthrough` passes unanswered queries on, and `forward` sends them upstream. In Kubernetes the same Corefile lives in the `coredns` ConfigMap.
09-Networking/05-Pre-requisite-Network-N:
### Introduction

Linux **network namespaces** isolate network stacks: each has its own interfaces, routes and ARP table. Containers use them for isolation.

### Create and use

```bash
ip netns add red
ip netns add blue
ip netns list
ip netns exec red ip link          # run a command inside
ip -n red link                     # shorter
```

The namespace sees none of the host's interfaces.

### Connect two namespaces with a virtual cable

```bash
ip link add veth-red type veth peer name veth-blue
ip link set veth-red netns red
ip link set veth-blue netns blue
ip -n red addr add 192.168.15.1/24 dev veth-red
ip -n blue addr add 192.168.15.2/24 dev veth-blue
ip -n red link set veth-red up
ip -n blue link set veth-blue up
ip netns exec red ping 192.168.15.2
```

### Many namespaces: a virtual bridge

For more than two, create a bridge switch on the host:

```bash
ip link add v-net-0 type bridge
ip link set dev v-net-0 up
ip link add veth-red type veth peer name veth-red-br
ip link set veth-red netns red
ip link set veth-red-br master v-net-0
ip -n red addr add 192.168.15.1/24 dev veth-red
ip -n red link set veth-red up
ip link set veth-red-br up
```

Give the bridge an IP so the host can reach namespaces: `ip addr add 192.168.15.5/24 dev v-net-0`.

### Reaching the outside

```bash
ip netns exec blue ip route add default via 192.168.15.5
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.15.0/24 -j MASQUERADE
```

### Reaching inwards (port forwarding)

```bash
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.15.2:80
```

### Key takeaways

- Namespace = isolated network stack; veth pairs + bridge + NAT connect it. This is what container runtimes automate.
09-Networking/06-Pre-requisite-Docker-Ne:
### Introduction

How Docker uses namespaces, bridges and NAT to network containers. Kubernetes uses similar ideas.

### Network modes

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `none` | No network |
| `host` | Shares the host's network (no isolation; port conflicts) |
| `bridge` (default) | Private internal network `172.17.0.0/16` via `docker0` bridge |

```bash
docker run --network none nginx
docker run --network host nginx
docker network ls
ip addr show docker0
```

### How bridge mode works

For each container Docker creates a namespace and a veth pair attached to the bridge. Containers on the bridge reach each other by IP.

### Port mapping

Containers are not reachable from outside by default. Publish ports:

```bash
docker run -p 8080:80 nginx
```

Docker adds an iptables NAT rule:

```
iptables -t nat -A DOCKER -j DNAT --dport 8080 --to-destination 172.17.0.3:80
```

```bash
iptables -nvL -t nat
```

### Key takeaways

- Bridge + veth + iptables NAT = Docker networking.
- Kubernetes needs a different model (every Pod reachable without NAT), supplied by CNI plugins.
09-Networking/07-Pre-requisite-CNI:
### Introduction

Every container runtime repeated the same networking steps. The **Container Network Interface (CNI)** defines a standard so runtimes and network plugins interoperate.

### The standard

For the runtime (kubelet/containerd): create a namespace, identify the network, invoke the plugin on **add** and **delete**, and handle the JSON config.

For the plugin: support `ADD`, `DEL`, `CHECK` commands, take container ID and namespace, assign IPs, set up routes, return results.

```
 runtime ──► plugin ADD(container id, netns, config) ──► IP, routes assigned
```

### Plugins

bridge, vlan, ipvlan, macvlan, host-device (built-in); Weave, Flannel, Calico, Cilium, Cisco ACI, VMware NSX and others (third-party).

**Docker does not implement CNI**; it uses its own CNM (container network model). That's why Kubernetes with Docker created its networking manually with `--network=none` and the CNI plugin.

### Key takeaways

- CNI = plugin standard for container networking; Kubernetes uses it.
09-Networking/08-Cluster-Networking:
### Introduction

What networking a Kubernetes cluster needs between its nodes and components.

### Node requirements

- Each node has at least one interface on the node network with an IP, a unique hostname and a unique MAC address.
- Required open ports:

| Port | Component | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 6443 | kube-apiserver | control plane |
| 10250 | kubelet API | all nodes |
| 10259 | kube-scheduler | control plane |
| 10257 | kube-controller-manager | control plane |
| 2379 | etcd client | control plane |
| 2380 | etcd peer | control plane |
| 30000–32767 | NodePort services | workers |

Firewalls and security groups must allow these. (In clusters with multiple control planes, ETCD ports are open between them.)

### Commands to explore

```bash
ip link ; ip addr
ip addr show eth0
ip route
netstat -nplt             # listening ports (or ss -tlnp)
netstat -anp | grep etcd
arp node01
```

### Notable details

- The API server listens on 6443, ETCD on 2379 (clients) and 2380 (peers). Because there are more client connections to 2379, etcd on multiple control planes needs both.
- The kubelet's port 10250 and the control plane component ports are used by health checks and metrics.

### Key takeaways

- Know the port table.
09-Networking/09-Practice-Test-Explore-E:
### How to approach this lab

Explore the interfaces, routes and ports of the lab cluster.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o wide                    # INTERNAL-IP
ip a | grep -B2 192.168                      # interface for that IP
ip link show eth0                            # MAC address
ip route
ip link show cni0 ; ip link show flannel.1
netstat -natulp | grep kube-scheduler
netstat -natulp | grep etcd | grep LISTEN
```

### Typical answers

| Question | How |
|---|---|
| Interface used for the cluster network | The one with the node's INTERNAL-IP |
| Default gateway | `ip route` default line |
| Port the scheduler listens on | `netstat -nplt \| grep scheduler` (10259) |
| ETCD ports | 2379 and 2380 (2379 has more connections) |
| CNI bridge / interface name | `ip link` (cni0, docker0, flannel.1) |

### Worked example

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o wide                    # INTERNAL-IP 192.168.121.x
ip -o -4 addr show | grep 192.168.121        # interface eth0
ip link show eth0 | grep link/ether          # MAC
ip route | grep default                      # gateway
ss -tlnp | grep -E "kube-sched|etcd"
```

Ports: scheduler 10259, controller manager 10257, etcd 2379 (client) and 2380 (peer). The etcd client port has more connections because every API server connects to it.
09-Networking/10-Pod-Networking:
### Introduction

Kubernetes expects a flat Pod network. The model:

- Every Pod gets its own IP.
- Pods on the same node can communicate.
- Pods on different nodes can communicate **without NAT**.

Kubernetes doesn't implement this; a CNI plugin does.

### Manual illustration

Each node gets a Pod subnet (e.g. 10.244.1.0/24, 10.244.2.0/24). On each node:

```
 node1                                node2
 ┌─────────────────┐                 ┌─────────────────┐
 │ bridge v-net-0  │                 │ bridge v-net-0  │
 │ 10.244.1.1/24   │                 │ 10.244.2.1/24   │
 │ pod 10.244.1.2  │                 │ pod 10.244.2.2  │
 └────────┬────────┘                 └────────┬────────┘
          └────────── node network ───────────┘
 routes: node1: 10.244.2.0/24 via node2 IP ; node2: 10.244.1.0/24 via node1 IP
```

### What the CNI script does

When a Pod is created, the runtime calls the plugin which:

1. Creates a veth pair.
2. Attaches one end to the Pod namespace and the other to the bridge.
3. Assigns an IP (from the node's Pod CIDR) and adds routes.
4. Brings the interfaces up.

On delete it removes them.

### Routes between nodes

Implemented as host routes, an overlay (VXLAN), or BGP (Calico). Plugins do this automatically.

### Key takeaways

- Flat Pod network, no NAT, with per-node Pod CIDRs.
09-Networking/11-CNI-in-Kubernetes:
### Introduction

How Kubernetes finds and calls the CNI plugin.

### Who invokes CNI

The container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) creates the Pod sandbox and calls the CNI plugin. The kubelet provides the configuration via the runtime settings.

### Where it's configured

```
/opt/cni/bin/               plugin executables (bridge, host-local, flannel, ...)
/etc/cni/net.d/             configuration files (first file alphabetically is used)
```

```bash
ls /opt/cni/bin
ls /etc/cni/net.d
cat /etc/cni/net.d/10-flannel.conflist
```

### A config

```json
{
  "cniVersion": "0.3.1",
  "name": "mynet",
  "type": "bridge",
  "bridge": "cni0",
  "isGateway": true,
  "ipMasq": true,
  "ipam": {
    "type": "host-local",
    "subnet": "10.244.0.0/16",
    "routes": [{ "dst": "0.0.0.0/0" }]
  }
}
```

The `type` is the plugin, `ipam` decides IP allocation, `isGateway` gives the bridge an IP, `ipMasq` enables NAT for outside access.

### Check which plugin runs

```bash
ps aux | grep kubelet           # container-runtime-endpoint
kubectl -n kube-system get pods # weave-net / calico / flannel
```

### Troubleshooting

- Nodes `NotReady` with "network plugin not ready: cni config uninitialized": no CNI installed.
- Pods stuck in `ContainerCreating` with errors about CNI: plugin Pods not running, or config missing.

### Key takeaways

- Binaries in `/opt/cni/bin`, config in `/etc/cni/net.d`.
09-Networking/12-CNI-weave:
### Introduction

Weave Net is a CNI plugin that creates an overlay network. A Weave agent runs on each node, they learn about each other and encapsulate traffic between nodes.

```
 node1: weave peer ◄═══ encapsulated traffic ═══► weave peer :node2
        pod A ──► weave bridge                      weave bridge ──► pod B
```

### Deploying

Weave runs as a DaemonSet, one Pod per node:

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://reweave.azurewebsites.net/k8s/v1.29/net.yaml
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep weave
kubectl logs -n kube-system weave-net-xxxxx -c weave
```

### Inspect

```bash
ip link | grep weave            # weave bridge
ip addr show weave
kubectl -n kube-system get ds weave-net
```

Default Pod network range `10.32.0.0/12`.

### Other CNI choices

| Plugin | Notes |
|---|---|
| Flannel | Simple overlay; **no NetworkPolicy** |
| Calico | BGP/routing; NetworkPolicy; popular |
| Cilium | eBPF; NetworkPolicy, observability |
| Weave | Overlay; NetworkPolicy support |

### Key takeaways

- Weave = DaemonSet overlay; check its Pods and bridge interface.
09-Networking/13-Practice-Test-CNI-weave:
### How to approach this lab

Identify which CNI the cluster uses and its settings.

### Commands

```bash
ls /etc/cni/net.d
cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist
ls /opt/cni/bin
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide
ps -aux | grep kubelet | grep -i container-runtime
ip link
```

### Typical answers

| Question | Where |
|---|---|
| Which plugin is configured | file name / `type` in `/etc/cni/net.d` |
| Binary executed | `/opt/cni/bin/<type>` |
| Which runtime | kubelet flag `--container-runtime-endpoint` |
| Pod subnet | `ipam.subnet` or `kubeadm` pod CIDR |

### Worked example

```bash
ls /etc/cni/net.d/                      # 10-weave.conflist
grep -E '"type"' /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist
ls /opt/cni/bin | head
ps aux | grep kubelet | grep -o "container-runtime-endpoint=[^ ]*"
kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep weave
```

The plugin binary a Pod uses is the one named by `type` (for Weave: `weave-net`, plus `weave-ipam`).
09-Networking/14-Practice-Test-Deploy-Ne:
### How to approach this lab

Pods are stuck because no CNI is installed. Deploy one (Weave) with the correct Pod CIDR.

### Steps

```bash
kubectl get pods                         # ContainerCreating
kubectl describe pod app                 # no CNI / network plugin not ready
kubectl apply -f <weave-net-manifest>
kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep weave
kubectl get pods -w
```

### Pod CIDR conflict

If the Weave default range overlaps with the node network, set `IPALLOC_RANGE` in the DaemonSet:

```yaml
containers:
- name: weave
  env:
  - name: IPALLOC_RANGE
    value: 10.32.0.0/16
```

```bash
kubectl edit ds weave-net -n kube-system
```

### Verify

Pods become `Running` and get IPs from the range; test connectivity between Pods.

### Worked example

Symptoms: new Pods stay in `ContainerCreating`; `kubectl describe pod` shows `network plugin is not ready: cni config uninitialized`.

```bash
ls /etc/cni/net.d            # empty
kubectl apply -f weave-daemonset.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l name=weave-net
kubectl get pods             # now Running
```

Check the Pod CIDR (`kubectl cluster-info dump | grep -m1 cluster-cidr`) and set `IPALLOC_RANGE` in the weave container env if the default range overlaps with your nodes.

### Common mistakes

- Applying a manifest meant for a different Kubernetes version.
- Leaving a previous CNI config in `/etc/cni/net.d` (the first file alphabetically wins).
09-Networking/15-ipam-weave:
### Introduction

IP Address Management (IPAM) decides how Pods receive unique IP addresses. The CNI plugin delegates to an IPAM plugin.

### Options

- **host-local**: each node has its own subnet and a local file tracks allocations. Simple; the cluster must carve out per-node ranges.
- **Weave's IPAM**: allocates from a shared range, split dynamically among peers. Default range `10.32.0.0/12` divided across nodes.
- **Calico IPAM**, cloud-specific IPAMs.

### Config

```json
"ipam": {
  "type": "host-local",
  "subnet": "10.244.1.0/24"
}
```

### Check

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}'
kubectl get pods -A -o wide     # Pod IPs
```

### Key takeaways

- IPAM ensures unique Pod IPs; the node CIDR (`--pod-network-cidr`, `--cluster-cidr`) matters.
09-Networking/16-Practice-Test-Networkin:
### How to approach this lab

Find the Weave agent details and which node a Pod is on.

### Commands

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep weave
kubectl logs -n kube-system weave-net-xxxx -c weave | grep -i ipalloc
ip addr show weave
ip route | grep weave
kubectl run busybox --image=busybox --command -- sleep 1000
kubectl get pods -o wide
```

### Typical answers

- Weave peers = number of nodes.
- Pod IP range = log line `ipalloc-range`.
- Default gateway for Pods on a node = the weave bridge IP.

### Worked example

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide | grep weave        # one per node
kubectl -n kube-system logs weave-net-xxxxx -c weave | grep -i ipalloc
ip addr show weave                                          # bridge IP on the node
kubectl run busybox --image=busybox --command -- sleep 1000
kubectl get pod busybox -o wide                             # node + Pod IP
ip route | grep weave
```

The default gateway inside Pods on a node is the weave bridge address on that node.
09-Networking/17-Service-Networking:
### Introduction

How Service IPs work. Services are cluster-wide virtual objects: no process, no interface. Kube-proxy on every node turns them into forwarding rules.

### Ranges

```
Pod network       10.244.0.0/16     (CNI)
Service network   10.96.0.0/12      (--service-cluster-ip-range on the API server)
```

The two ranges must not overlap with each other or the node network.

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane | grep service-cluster-ip-range
```

### Creation flow

```
 Service created ─► kube-proxy on each node watches the API
                  ─► adds rules: ClusterIP:port → Pod IP:port
```

### Types as rules

- **ClusterIP**: rule on each node for internal use.
- **NodePort**: also listens on a port on each node (30000–32767).

### See the rules

```bash
iptables -t nat -L -n | grep db-service
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES | head
```

Rule comments show `default/db-service`. Log: `/var/log/kube-proxy.log` or Pod logs.

### Mode options

kube-proxy `--proxy-mode`: `iptables` (default), `ipvs`, `nftables`.

### Key takeaways

- Service IPs are virtual and implemented as NAT rules by kube-proxy.
09-Networking/18-Practice-Test-Service-N:
### How to approach this lab

Discover ranges and kube-proxy configuration.

### Commands

```bash
ip addr show eth0                                    # node network
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane | grep service-cluster
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep proxy
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-xxxxx | head       # "Using iptables Proxier"
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kube-proxy -o yaml | grep -E "mode|clusterCIDR"
iptables -t nat -L | grep db-service
kubectl get ds -n kube-system
```

### Typical answers

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Service IP range | API server `--service-cluster-ip-range` |
| Pod IP range | CNI config / `clusterCIDR` / pod CIDR |
| Proxy mode | kube-proxy Pod logs or ConfigMap (default iptables) |
| Where does kube-proxy run | DaemonSet, one per node |

### Worked example

```bash
ip addr show eth0                                              # node network
kubectl cluster-info dump | grep -m1 service-cluster-ip-range
kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/kube-proxy | grep -i proxier     # "Using iptables Proxier"
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | head
```

Rules show the Service IP, port and the chain that leads to Pod endpoints.

### Common mistakes

- Confusing the Pod CIDR with the Service CIDR.
- Looking for kube-proxy as a systemd service (it's a DaemonSet in kubeadm clusters).
09-Networking/19-DNS-in-kubernetes:
### Introduction

Kubernetes runs an internal DNS server so Pods find Services by name.

### Service records

For a Service `web-service` in namespace `apps`:

```
web-service                              (same namespace)
web-service.apps
web-service.apps.svc
web-service.apps.svc.cluster.local       (fully qualified)
```

Root domain `cluster.local`, then `svc`, then namespace.

### Pod records

Not created by default; if enabled, Pods get names such as `10-244-2-5.apps.pod.cluster.local` (dots replaced by dashes).

### How Pods use it

The kubelet writes `/etc/resolv.conf` in each Pod:

```
nameserver 10.96.0.10          # the kube-dns Service IP
search apps.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5
```

The search list makes short names work. `ndots:5` means names with fewer than five dots try the search domains first.

### Test

```bash
kubectl run test --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup web-service
kubectl exec -it pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl run test --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup web-service.apps.svc.cluster.local
```

### Key takeaways

- `service.namespace.svc.cluster.local`; resolv.conf search domains make short names work.
09-Networking/20-CoreDNS-in-Kubernetes:
### Introduction

CoreDNS is the cluster DNS. It runs as a Deployment (two replicas) in `kube-system` behind the `kube-dns` Service.

### Components

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get deploy coredns
kubectl -n kube-system get svc kube-dns
kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml
```

### Corefile ConfigMap

```
.:53 {
    errors
    health { lameduck 5s }
    ready
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
       pods insecure
       fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
       ttl 30
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
    loadbalance
}
```

- `kubernetes` plugin handles `cluster.local`.
- `forward . /etc/resolv.conf` sends everything else to the node's resolvers.
- Edit the ConfigMap and CoreDNS reloads (`reload` plugin) or restart the Pods: `kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy coredns`.

### How Pods find CoreDNS

The kubelet sets `--cluster-dns=10.96.0.10` and `--cluster-domain=cluster.local` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`:

```bash
grep -A2 clusterDNS /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
```

### Troubleshooting DNS

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl get endpoints kube-dns -n kube-system
kubectl run t --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default
```

Common causes: CoreDNS Pods down, wrong Corefile, loop plugin detecting a loop with `/etc/resolv.conf` pointing to itself, NetworkPolicy blocking port 53, wrong `clusterDNS`.

### Key takeaways

- CoreDNS Deployment + `kube-dns` Service + Corefile ConfigMap.
